chunks: "I'd start by asking what it has to measure: the signal range and bandwidth, how much resolution or accuracy I need, the supply voltage, and the power and cost budget.
Say it's a sensor channel on a 3. 3 volts board, 0 to 3. 3 volts, up to 10 kilohertz, and I want about 1 millivolts resolution. From that: 3.
3 volts over 1 millivolts is 3300 levels, so 12 bits gives me 0. 8 millivolts steps. Nyquist says more than 20 kS/s, and I'd go to 100 kS/s to relax the anti-alias filter.
That's low resolution and modest speed, so a SAR is the natural choice: one comparator, a capacitor DAC that also does the sampling, 12 comparisons per conversion.
At 100 kS/s with about 15 clock cycles per conversion, I need a clock of about 1. 5 megahertz. Easy. Then I'd size the pieces.
The sampling capacitor needs kT/C noise well under an LSB, and a few picofarads gives about 20 to 30 microvolts.
The input has to charge it to half an LSB within the sampling window, about nine time constants for 12 bits.
The reference needs a decoupling capacitor, and I'd put an RC low-pass filter in front of the ADC.
If I had to build one from parts, I'd use the microcontroller: an R-2R DAC on eight GPIO pins, a comparator, and firmware that does the binary search.
It would be slower and only about 8 bits with 0. 1% resistors, but it works. Finally I'd verify it with a slow ramp for DNL and INL and a sine wave for SNR and effective bits."
